title: Structural Design Patterns: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge
summary: Quick revision notes on the six structural design patterns: the intent and structure of each, when to reach for it, and how the look-alike pairs differ. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Structural Patterns Mental Model
points: Structural patterns compose classes and objects into larger structures without changing their behaviour contracts; they favour composition over inheritance
Most share one skeleton: a wrapper holds a reference to a wrapped object and forwards calls; the patterns differ in intent, not in shape
Interface relationship decides the pattern: wrapper changes the interface (Adapter, Facade), keeps it identical (Decorator, Proxy, Composite), or splits abstraction from implementation (Bridge)
One-line intents: Adapter converts, Decorator adds, Facade simplifies, Proxy controls access, Composite treats tree and leaf alike, Bridge decouples abstraction from implementation
Quick test when two patterns look alike: ask what the wrapper is for (convert, add, simplify, guard, aggregate), not how it is built

chapters.title: Adapter and Facade: Changing the Interface
points: Adapter: client expects interface Target, existing class Adaptee has an incompatible one; the Adapter implements Target and translates each call to the Adaptee
Object adapter holds the adaptee by composition (preferred, works with subclasses); class adapter inherits from it via multiple inheritance, which is rare
Example: class XmlToJsonAdapter implements JsonSource { constructor(private xml: XmlSource) {} read() { return toJson(this.xml.read()); } }
Facade: one simplified entry point over a complex subsystem (e.g. VideoConverter.convert(file, 'mp4') hides codec, bitrate and audio classes); subsystem classes stay publicly usable

Adapter vs Facade: Adapter makes one existing interface match one the client already expects, Facade defines a new simpler interface over many classes; common mistake is a Facade that grows into a god object holding business logic

chapters.title: Decorator and Proxy: Same Interface, Different Intent
points: Decorator: wraps an object with the same interface and adds behaviour before or after delegating; decorators stack, e.g. new Gzip(new Encrypt(new FileStream()))
Decorator example: Java BufferedReader(new FileReader(f)), or Python @decorator functions adding logging or caching around a call
Proxy: stand-in with the same interface that controls access to the real object; variants are virtual (lazy load), protection (permission check), remote (network stub) and caching
Decorator vs Proxy: Decorator is chosen and stacked by the client to add features, Proxy usually manages the real object's lifecycle or access itself and is often invisible to the client

Mistakes: decorator order changes results (encrypt then compress differs from compress then encrypt); proxy that swallows errors or breaks the interface; using subclassing where decorators avoid a class explosion

chapters.title: Composite and Bridge: Hierarchies and Abstractions
points: Composite: Component interface implemented by both Leaf and Composite; Composite stores child Components and forwards calls to them, so client treats one object and a tree identically (e.g. file and folder, size())
Composite example: Folder.size() = sum(child.size() for child in children); File.size() returns its own bytes; add(), remove() live on Composite and the trade-off is transparency vs safety
Bridge: split a class into Abstraction and Implementor hierarchies joined by composition, so both vary independently (Shape with Renderer: Circle/Square x Vector/Raster, M+N classes instead of M×N)
Bridge vs Adapter: Bridge is designed up front to separate two dimensions of change, Adapter is applied after the fact to make incompatible existing classes work together
Mistakes: Bridge used when only one dimension varies; confusing Bridge with the Strategy pattern, which swaps an algorithm rather than a whole implementation hierarchy

chapters.title: Choosing Between the Six Patterns
points: Decision table: incompatible interface -> Adapter; simplify a subsystem -> Facade; add behaviour dynamically -> Decorator; control access or lazy-load -> Proxy; tree of uniform parts -> Composite; two independent dimensions of variation -> Bridge
Same-interface group (Decorator, Proxy, Composite) vs new-interface group (Adapter, Facade): checking whether the wrapper's interface equals the wrapped one narrows the choice

Real-code examples: Java BufferedReader over FileReader (Decorator), JS Proxy object (Proxy), React component tree (Composite), jQuery over DOM (Facade), ORM driver layer (Bridge), Node stream wrappers (Decorator)
Over-engineering: do not apply a pattern for one implementation, or when a plain function or direct call is enough
Patterns combine: a Facade may use Adapters internally, a Composite tree may be wrapped by Decorators, a Proxy can front a Facade

chapters.title: Structural Patterns Cheat Sheet
points: Adapter: convert interface A to B; wraps one object; the interface changes; example: legacy SDK wrapper
Decorator: add behaviour; same interface; stackable; example: Gzip(Encrypt(Stream))
Facade: simplify a subsystem; new simpler interface; example: VideoConverter.convert()
Proxy: control access; same interface; virtual, protection, remote, cache; example: lazy image loader
Composite and Bridge: Composite = tree where leaf and group share one interface; Bridge = abstraction and implementation vary independently, M+N not M×N
